checklist.name: granulomatous dermatitis or skin rash

quotes.text: skin rash is the first symptom to appear, usually in the first year of life
a non-caseating granulomatous inflammatory infiltrate located in the dermis is characteristic
The initial eruption presents as red‐brown monomorphous papules with no epidermal changes

checklist.why: Part of the defining triad and usually the first sign, in infancy.

checklist.name: arthritis or joint synovitis

quotes.text: Data from the Blau international registry revealed polyarticular arthritis at presentation in 96% of patients
Joint involvement presents as joint effusion, due to granulomatous synovitis and tenosynovitis

checklist.why: Part of the defining triad; boggy polyarthritis of peripheral joints.

checklist.name: tenosynovitis

quotes.text: Tenosynovitis is equally a characteristic feature; tendon sheaths appear enlarged on examination

checklist.why: Named as characteristic, and distinct from joint synovitis (tendon sheaths).

checklist.name: camptodactyly

quotes.text: more than fifty percent of Blau patients had articular deformities, with camptodactyly (flexion contracture at PIP joints) being most commonly observed

checklist.why: The most common articular deformity, often early and out of proportion to synovitis.

checklist.name: uveitis

quotes.text: Uveitis presents as an insidious granulomatous iridocyclitis with posterior uveitis in many patients, and a potential evolution into a severe panuveitis with multifocal choroiditis
about 15-20% of patients with Blau syndrome do not develop eye disease
with ocular involvement appearing around age 4 years

checklist.why: Part of the defining triad; absent in a minority, so its absence matters too.

checklist.name: cataract

quotes.text: More than one-third had ocular complications (including band keratopathy, increased intraocular pressure, cataracts, optic atrophy, macular edema and retinal detachment)
long‐term complications of cataracts, glaucoma

checklist.why: A common ocular complication named by both reviews.

checklist.name: glaucoma or raised intraocular pressure

quotes.text: More than one-third had ocular complications (including band keratopathy, increased intraocular pressure, cataracts, optic atrophy, macular edema and retinal detachment)
cataracts, glaucoma, posterior synechiae

checklist.why: An ocular complication named by both reviews, distinct from cataract.

checklist.name: visual impairment or blindness

quotes.text: almost two-thirds had visual loss
extremely poor visual outcomes or blindness have been reported in more than half of the children

checklist.why: The main morbidity of Blau uveitis; case reports state visual acuity or blindness.

checklist.name: fever

quotes.text: Most notably fever and erythema nodosum were detected quite commonly in this Spanish cohort
the p.R587C pathogenic variant was associated with a higher incidence of fever

checklist.why: The commonest extra-triad feature; Wang links it to a genotype (p.R587C).

checklist.name: erythema nodosum or panniculitis

quotes.text: Erythema nodosum has been mentioned frequently; in fact it is the second most common cutaneous manifestation of Blau syndrome
additional manifestations, such as fever, panniculitis, and granulomatous lymphadenopathy

checklist.why: Second most common skin manifestation, distinct from the papular granulomatous rash.

checklist.name: lymphadenopathy

quotes.text: We found generalized lymphadenopathies and splenomegaly in more than one-fifth of patients in the Blau prospective study
Systemic manifestations, including lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, occur in a large subset of patients

checklist.why: Reticuloendothelial involvement, in over a fifth of the prospective cohort.

checklist.name: hepatomegaly or hepatic granulomas

quotes.text: Hepatomegaly can be seen, but liver enzymes and liver function are mostly normal
We have reported hepatic granulomas on a liver biopsy in a child with Blau syndrome
Systemic manifestations, including lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, occur in a large subset of patients

checklist.why: Liver involvement, named by both reviews.

checklist.name: splenomegaly

quotes.text: We found generalized lymphadenopathies and splenomegaly in more than one-fifth of patients in the Blau prospective study
Systemic manifestations, including lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, occur in a large subset of patients

checklist.why: Reticuloendothelial involvement named by both reviews.

checklist.name: vasculitis (large-vessel arteritis, aortitis or leukocytoclastic vasculitis)

quotes.text: The association between large vessel vasculitis and Blau syndrome was reported before the genetic mutation was discovered
Also leukocytoclastic vasculitis has been documented in a patient with Blau
Systemic manifestations, such as granulomatous lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and large vessel vasculitis, may emerge in adolescence

checklist.why: Highlighted as an extra-triad manifestation of particular importance (Takayasu-like arteritis, aortitis).

checklist.name: systemic hypertension

quotes.text: two young patients from the international registry developed severe systemic hypertension
Hence pulmonary and systemic hypertension may be seen in the course of Blau syndrome

checklist.why: Flagged by Wouters as requiring vigilance.

checklist.name: interstitial lung disease

quotes.text: Interstitial lung disease was observed in three additional patients of the prospective Blau study
he developed cervical lymphadenopathy and interstitial lung disease

checklist.why: Lung involvement, now accepted as part of the phenotype (Wouters).

checklist.name: granulomatous nephritis or renal failure

quotes.text: granulomatous glomerular and interstitial nephritis, interstitial lung disease, arterial hypertension, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, hepatic granulomas, splenic involvement and chronic renal failure
Renal involvement has been described as an interstitial nephritis in the context of Blau syndrome

checklist.why: Renal involvement, histologically documented as granulomatous nephritis.

checklist.name: pericarditis

quotes.text: interstitial lung disease, arterial hypertension, pericarditis

checklist.why: The only cardiac (serosal) manifestation named in the reviews' expanded-phenotype list.

checklist.name: cranial or other neuropathy (facial palsy)

quotes.text: Cranial neuropathies, particularly facial palsy have also been documented in Blau
leukocytoclastic vasculitis, transient neuropathies

checklist.why: The neurological manifestation described; central nervous system involvement is not.

checklist.name: elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP)

quotes.text: infliximab normalized inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C‐reactive protein quickly
marked improvements in laboratory parameters, including ESR, CRP, IL‐6, and TNF‐α

checklist.why: The laboratory sign of systemic inflammation that case reports commonly state.

left_out: ichthyosis-like or scaly skin changes, tan 'dirty' pigmentation, follicular atrophoderma or poikiloderma: stages or residua of the granulomatous rash, so they would sit inside item 1
skin nodules: Wang calls them common, but they overlap with both the granulomatous rash and erythema nodosum
eruption or granuloma at the BCG vaccination site: described as a trigger (9 of 50 cases in a cited series), not a disease feature
multifocal choroiditis, panuveitis, iridocyclitis, keratic precipitates, synechiae, iris nodules, vitreous inflammation: forms or signs of uveitis, inside item 5

band keratopathy, optic atrophy, macular edema, retinal detachment, keratitis, episcleritis, conjunctivitis, papilledema and other listed ocular findings: individually less central; the eye already has four items
sialadenitis: named only once, in a list of expanded manifestations
pulmonary hypertension: one unpublished fatal case only
pulmonary embolism: named only once, in a list
central nervous system involvement or seizures: Wouters says it has not been reported and a published seizure case was not clearly related
joint destruction or erosions: Wouters says rare; Wang and the Zhong study cited by Wang call arthritis destructive; not a clear feature to score
negative antinuclear antibodies: a pertinent negative favouring the diagnosis, not a feature of the disease
non-caseating granulomas on biopsy: the defining histology, the diagnostic test rather than a clinical feature
pain, functional impairment (CHAQ/HAQ): outcomes rather than features
elevated S100A12, IL-6 or TNF-alpha: research markers rather than routine case-report findings
lichenoid eruption, renal artery stenosis/renal vasculitis (inside item 14), sinus of Valsalva aneurysm and cardiac infiltration: single cases or cited only in reference titles
notes: Sources: Wouters et al. 2014 (PMID 25136265) and Wang et al. 2025 (PMID 40456554), and nothing else. From Wouters only: tenosynovitis, camptodactyly, systemic hypertension, granulomatous nephritis or renal failure, pericarditis, cranial or other neuropathy. From Wang only: elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), which Wang mentions only through treatment normalizing them, not as a stated feature; this is the weakest item. From both: granulomatous dermatitis, arthritis, uveitis, cataract, glaucoma or raised intraocular pressure, visual impairment or blindness, fever, erythema nodosum or panniculitis (erythema nodosum from Wouters, panniculitis from Wang), lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly or hepatic granulomas, splenomegaly, vasculitis, interstitial lung disease. Conflicts: Wang's Table 3 lists 'No pulmonary involvement' as a pertinent negative for Blau syndrome, while Wouters and Wang's own text describe interstitial lung disease; it is kept. Several items (pericarditis, renal, hypertension, neuropathy) are rare, named in Wouters' expanded-manifestations paragraph; they are there to span organ systems and will mostly be 'not reported'. Visual impairment could be seen as an outcome; kept because both reviews stress it and case reports state visual acuity. Wang's hyphens are U+2010; quotes copy them exactly.
